title: Scattered grain (Didache 9)
hook: an early communion prayer: as grain once scattered on the hills became one loaf, gather your church
tomorrow: two days circled on a calendar, three marks on a clock. why?

segments.voice: That was the week: Tertius holding Paul's pen, a hymn inside Philippians, the household codes read in context, Phebe first on the last page, letters read as if to you, and the Didache's fork. Yesterday's line: the way of life.
screen: `THE WAY OF LIFE.` → `A WEEK OF LETTERS, AND A FORK.`

segments.voice: Bread from the store comes sliced and bagged, with no field in sight. But wheat doesn't grow in loaves. It grows on hillsides, stalk by stalk, field after field. To get one loaf, someone has to gather grain from all over, grind it together, and bake it as one. The Didache looked at a loaf on the table and heard a prayer in it.
screen: `SLICED AND BAGGED.` → `WHEAT ON THE HILLSIDES.` → `A PRAYER IN A LOAF.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine of the Didache tells a church how to give thanks at its meal. It calls the meal the eucharist, a Greek word for thanksgiving. Thanks over the cup first, then over the broken bread. Then the picture: as this broken bread was scattered over the hills, and was gathered together and became one, so let your church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom. Paul has a close cousin of the thought: "For we being many are one bread, and one body." And John says Jesus would "gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad." Readers differ on what kind of meal chapter nine describes. Churches also understand the bread differently, Catholics and Orthodox Christians one way, Protestant churches in their own ways. The picture crosses those lines. Many grains, one loaf.
screen: `EUCHARIST: THANKSGIVING.` · `THE CUP, THEN THE BROKEN BREAD.` · `GATHERED FROM THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `WE BEING MANY ARE ONE BREAD.` · then, large: `SCATTERED, THEN ONE LOAF.`

segments.voice: If there's bread nearby, hold a piece and smell it before you eat; if not, bring a loaf to mind. Think of the grain from many stalks and fields that is now one, and if you pray, you can give thanks over it with the Didache's picture in mind.
Scattered grain. The Didache's picture of a church spread out like grain on the hills, and gathered like one loaf.
Keep this one: scattered, then one loaf, the grain still many and the bread still one. Seven days, gathered.

howItsDone: Christians share bread and cup at communion, the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper, and some churches still pray over the bread with words close to the Didache's picture of scattered grain made one.
